Thanks for that information. Riya's fever is mild (100.8°F/38.2°C) and she's acting well — playing, drinking normally, and alert. With just a little runny nose and no other symptoms, this looks like a **common viral cold or mild upper respiratory infection**. **What to do now:** • **Keep her comfortable** — offer plenty of fluids (water, soup, diluted juice). • **For the fever**, you can give **paracetamol or ibuprofen** if she seems uncomfortable. Use as directed on the label or by a pharmacist for her age/weight. • **Rest** — let her play quietly and rest as needed. • The runny nose and fever should improve on their own over the next few days. **When to seek urgent care:** Watch for any of these warning signs: • Fever above 104°F (40°C), or fever lasting more than 3 days • Difficulty breathing, fast breathing, or wheezing • Unusual drowsiness, difficulty waking, or not responding normally • Refusing to drink or signs of dehydration (very dry mouth, no tears, no urine for many hours) • Severe headache, stiff neck, or persistent vomiting • Rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass against it • She becomes much more unwell or you're worried This is not a diagnosis — just guidance to help you decide on care. If anything changes or you're concerned, don't hesitate to see a doctor.

With just a little runny nose and no other symptoms, this looks like a **common viral cold or mild upper respiratory infection**. **What to do now:** • **Keep her comfortable** — offer plenty of fluids (water, soup, diluted juice). • **For the fever**, you can give **paracetamol or ibuprofen** if she seems uncomfortable. User: what's the normal adult dose of ibuprofen in mg, and how many times a day can you take it?
Q → kind info · about — · 7394 ms
For adults, ibuprofen is commonly available as 200 mg or 400 mg tablets. **General guidance:** - A typical single dose is 200–400 mg - It can usually be taken every 4–6 hours as needed - The maximum daily dose is generally 1200 mg in 24 hours for over-the-counter use (higher doses may be prescribed by a doctor) **Important:** - Always follow the instructions on the packet or as advised by a pharmacist - Take it with food or milk to reduce the chance of stomach upset - Don't exceed the recommended dose or duration without medical advice - Avoid ibuprofen if you have certain conditions (stomach ulcers, severe heart or kidney problems, are pregnant in the third trimester, or are allergic to NSAIDs) - Check with a pharmacist if you're taking other medicines, as ibuprofen can interact with some medications If you're thinking about taking ibuprofen for yourself or someone in your household, I'm happy to help you figure out whether it's appropriate for your situation. Just let me know what's going on!

For Riya (3 years old), paracetamol syrup dosing depends on her weight, which is the safest way to dose. Here's the general guidance: **Dosing:** - **If you know her weight**: 15 mg per kg of body weight per dose - **Typical 3-year-old weight (around 14-16 kg)**: Usually 5-7.5 mL of standard paracetamol syrup (120 mg/5 mL strength), but check the label as strengths vary **How often:** - Every 4-6 hours as needed - Maximum 4 doses in 24 hours - Leave at least 4 hours between doses **Important:** - Always check the concentration on your bottle (it should say mg per mL or mg per 5 mL) - Use the measuring device that comes with the medicine - Don't give more than the maximum daily dose - If you're unsure about the dose or Riya's weight, ask a pharmacist — they can calculate the exact amount for you Is Riya unwell at the moment? Q → kind assessment · urgency urgent · escalate True · about Sunita · episode e_ce4e2d59 · 20961 ms
**This is an emergency. Heavy bleeding that won't stop with pressure needs immediate medical attention.** **What to do RIGHT NOW:** 1. **Keep firm, direct pressure on the wound** with a clean cloth or bandage. Don't keep lifting it to check - maintain constant pressure for at least 10-15 minutes. 2. **Elevate her hand** above the level of her heart if possible. 3. **Go to the nearest emergency department immediately** or **call your local emergency number** for an ambulance, especially if: - The bleeding is spurting or won't slow down - She feels faint, dizzy, or weak - The cut is very deep or you can see tissue/bone 4. If blood soaks through the cloth, add more on top - don't remove the original. Do not waste time cleaning the wound deeply or trying home remedies. Sunita needs medical care now to stop the bleeding and assess whether she needs stitches, and to check for any damage to tendons, nerves, or blood vessels. Please get her to emergency care immediately.

**You need to see a doctor urgently, ideally today.** Chest tightness that comes on with physical activity (like climbing stairs) and goes away with rest is a classic warning sign of **angina** — reduced blood flow to the heart. Given that you're 45 and your father had a heart attack at age 50, this needs to be checked right away. **What to do now:** - Contact your GP today, or go to an urgent care centre or emergency department. Explain your symptoms — they will likely want to do an ECG (heart tracing) and possibly blood tests. - **Do not** wait to see if it gets better on its own. - Avoid strenuous activity until you've been assessed. **Go to the emergency department immediately or call emergency services if you experience:** - Chest pain or tightness that is severe, lasts more than a few minutes, or doesn't go away with rest - Pain that spreads to your jaw, neck, arms, back or stomach - Shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness or feeling faint - Any chest discomfort that feels different or worse than what you've been having This could be angina or another heart condition, but only a doctor can assess you properly with tests. This is not a diagnosis, but these symptoms with your family history warrant urgent medical review.

Q → kind assessment · urgency self_care · escalate False · about Riya · episode e_50f3ac4e · 20160 ms
Thank you for those details. Riya's fever of 100.8°F with a mild runny nose and otherwise normal behaviour sounds like a **common viral cold**. It's very reassuring that she's playing and active. **What to do now:** • **Fluids:** Make sure she drinks plenty of water, diluted juice, or soup. • **Rest:** Let her rest when she wants to, but no need to keep her in bed if she's playful. • **Fever comfort:** If the fever is making her uncomfortable, you can give **paracetamol** (acetaminophen) or **ibuprofen** for children, following the dosage on the label for her age and weight. Don't give both at the same time unless advised by a doctor. • **Cool measures:** Light clothing and a lukewarm sponge bath can help her feel better. Most viral colds get better on their own in 5–7 days. **When to see a doctor soon (within 24 hours):** • Fever lasting more than 3 days • She becomes less active, refuses to drink, or seems very unwell • Fever goes away and then comes back **Seek urgent care if:** • Fever goes above 104°F (40°C) • Trouble breathing, fast breathing, or noisy breathing • Severe headache or stiff neck • Persistent vomiting or signs of dehydration (dry mouth, no tears, very little urine) • A rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass against it • She becomes very drowsy, unresponsive, or difficult to wake This is not a diagnosis — if you're worried or things change, don't hesitate to see a doctor.

For Riya (3 years old), paracetamol syrup dosing depends on her weight, which is the safest way to dose. Here's the general guidance: **Dosing:** - **If you know her weight**: 15 mg per kg of body weight per dose - **Typical 3-year-old weight (around 14-16 kg)**: Usually 5-7.5 mL of standard paracetamol syrup (120 mg/5 mL strength), but check the label as strengths vary **How often:** - Every 4-6 hours as needed - Maximum 4 doses in 24 hours - Leave at least 4 hours between doses **Important:** - Always check the concentration on your bottle (it should say mg per mL or mg per 5 mL) - Use the measuring device that comes with the medicine - Don't give more than the maximum daily dose - If you're unsure about the dose or Riya's weight, ask a pharmacist — they can calculate the exact amount for you Is Riya unwell at the moment? Q → kind assessment · urgency self_care · escalate False · about Ved · episode e_4c3ebd39 · 19595 ms
**What it might be:** Ved most likely has a **common cold** or minor nasal congestion. This is very common in babies and usually caused by a virus. The excellent signs are that he's breathing normally, feeding well, staying happy and hydrated—these tell me he's coping well with the stuffiness. **What to do now:** **Home care:** - **Saline nose drops:** Use baby saline drops (available at pharmacies) to help clear his nose. Put 1-2 drops in each nostril before feeds to make feeding easier. - **Upright position:** Hold him upright or slightly elevated during and after feeds—this can help with drainage. - **Humidity:** A cool mist humidifier in his room, or sitting with him in a steamy bathroom for a few minutes, can help loosen mucus. - **Keep feeding:** Continue regular feeds—breast milk or formula will keep him hydrated. - **Comfort:** Extra cuddles and comfort as needed! Stuffy noses in babies usually clear up on their own within 7-10 days. **When to seek urgent help** (go to the emergency department or call your doctor immediately) if Ved: - Has fast, difficult breathing or you hear wheezing - Refuses feeds or drinks much less than usual - Has fewer wet nappies (dehydration) - Develops a fever (38°C or higher—important for babies under 6 months) - Becomes very sleepy or hard to wake - Develops blue or pale lips or skin - The stuffiness lasts more than 10-14 days This is not a diagnosis, just guidance on what Ved's symptoms might mean and when to seek care.

Q → kind assessment · urgency self_care · escalate False · about Arjun · episode e_8aefa74f · 16954 ms
Good news — this sounds like a **common cold** or mild upper respiratory viral infection. No fever and a mild scratchy throat are reassuring signs. **What to do now:** - Continue with warm fluids like honey water, which soothes the throat - Stay hydrated (plenty of water) - Steam inhalation can help with the blocked nose (a bowl of hot water, lean over with a towel over your head, 5-10 minutes, 2-3 times a day) - You can take paracetamol if you develop a headache or body aches - Rest when possible - Throat lozenges or gargling with warm salt water may help the scratchiness Most colds improve on their own in 5-7 days. The blocked nose and sore throat should gradually get better over the next few days. **Watch for these warning signs and see a doctor if you develop:** - High fever (above 101°F/38.3°C) or fever lasting more than 3 days - Severe or worsening throat pain, especially on one side only, or difficulty swallowing - Trouble breathing or shortness of breath - Symptoms that get much worse after a few days or don't improve after 10 days - Severe headache, ear pain, or facial pain - Persistent cough with green or bloody phlegm This is not a diagnosis, just guidance to help you manage at home. If you're concerned or things change, don't hesitate to reach out.

User: my mother has been a little forgetful for the past couple of years, she misplaces her keys and glasses sometimes
Q → kind info · about Kamala · 11948 ms
At 80 years old, some mild forgetfulness like occasionally misplacing keys or glasses can be a normal part of ageing. It's good that you're keeping an eye on it. **When to be concerned:** If you notice any of these changes, it would be worth having her assessed by a doctor: - The memory problems are getting noticeably worse over weeks or months - She's forgetting recent conversations or repeating questions multiple times - She's getting lost in familiar places or confused about time and dates - She's having trouble with everyday tasks she used to manage (cooking, managing money, taking medications) - Changes in personality, mood, or judgment - Difficulty finding words or following conversations - Withdrawing from social activities For now, simple things can help: keeping keys and glasses in the same spot each time, using labels or lists, staying mentally and socially active, and managing any other health conditions well. Is there anything specific that's worrying you about her memory, or has anything changed recently?
turn 1 · Sat 3 Oct 2026, 12:02 PM IST
User: nothing sudden, she manages her daily routine fine and still cooks and goes for walks
Q → kind info · about Kamala · 9470 ms
That's reassuring to hear. If she's managing her daily routine independently, cooking, and getting out for walks, those are all good signs that her cognitive function is holding up well. **What you can do:** - Keep monitoring gently over time. Watch for any changes in her ability to manage finances, take medications correctly, or handle her usual tasks - Encourage activities that keep her mind active (reading, puzzles, social interaction) - Regular physical activity like her walks is excellent for brain health - Make sure any chronic conditions (blood pressure, diabetes) are well-controlled **When to see a doctor:** If you notice the forgetfulness becoming more frequent or she starts having trouble with tasks she's always managed, or if she becomes confused or disoriented, then it would be time for a proper assessment. For now, it sounds like age-appropriate memory changes rather than something to worry about. You're doing the right thing by staying aware.

Thanks for those details, Arjun. Your symptoms — blocked nose, scratchy throat, and slight dry cough since yesterday, with no fever — are most likely from a **common cold** or a mild viral upper respiratory infection. **What to do now:** - **Rest** and drink plenty of fluids (water, warm herbal teas with honey, soups) - **Steam inhalation** can help ease the blocked nose - **Gargle** with warm salt water for the scratchy throat (half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water) - You can use **paracetamol or ibuprofen** as directed on the label if you develop any discomfort or mild headache - Throat lozenges or honey (a spoonful) may soothe the throat - Over-the-counter decongestants or saline nasal sprays can help with the blocked nose if needed Most colds improve on their own in 5-7 days. You should be able to manage this at home. **Seek urgent care if:** - You develop a high fever (above 38.3°C or 101°F) that lasts more than 3 days - Your throat becomes very painful or you have trouble swallowing - You have difficulty breathing - Symptoms get much worse after 5-7 days or last more than 10 days - You develop severe headache, stiff neck, or a rash This is not a diagnosis — if you're concerned or things change, don't hesitate to check in with a doctor.

**What this is likely to be:** Anaya most likely has **gastroenteritis** (a tummy bug) — possibly viral or bacterial, or food poisoning. The combination of vomiting, watery diarrhoea, and low-grade fever is very typical. The main concern at her age is **dehydration**. **What you should do now:** **See a doctor today** — either visit your paediatrician or a clinic within the next few hours. Here's why: - Anaya has only urinated once since this morning (it's now past 1 PM), which suggests she's getting **dehydrated**. - She's had 4 episodes of vomiting and 2 watery stools, and you're not sure if she's keeping fluids down. - At 2 years old, toddlers can become dehydrated quickly with vomiting and diarrhoea. **While you arrange to see the doctor:** - Keep offering **very small, frequent sips** of fluids (ideally ORS — oral rehydration solution — if you can get some; otherwise water, coconut water, or diluted dal water). - Offer a teaspoon or two every few minutes rather than a full cup at once. - Don't force food, but if she wants to eat, offer bland foods like rice, banana, toast. - Avoid fruit juices and sugary drinks; they can make diarrhoea worse. **Seek urgent care (emergency department) if:** - She doesn't urinate for another 6 hours total, or the urine is very dark - She becomes very drowsy, floppy, or hard to wake - She can't keep down even tiny sips and keeps vomiting everything - You notice no tears when she cries, or her mouth and tongue are very dry - She has blood in her vomit or stool - Severe tummy pain - Sunken eyes or the soft spot on her head looks sunken It's good that she's still playing a bit — that's a reassuring sign — but the reduced urine output means she needs medical assessment today. This is not a diagnosis, just guidance on what to do next. The doctor will examine her properly and may give treatment to prevent further dehydration.

Good news—what you're describing sounds like **age-related memory changes**, which are very common and can be part of normal aging. The fact that Kamala's forgetfulness has been stable over the past couple of years (not worsening), she manages her daily routine well, still cooks, and goes for walks are all reassuring signs. Occasionally misplacing keys or glasses is something many people experience at any age, and as long as she can find them again and her day-to-day life isn't affected, this is usually not a cause for concern. **What to do now:** - **Keep an eye on it.** If you notice the forgetfulness getting worse, affecting her ability to do everyday tasks, or if she starts having trouble recognizing people or places, then it would be worth seeing a doctor. - **Healthy habits help:** Encourage her to keep up the walks (physical activity is great for brain health), stay socially connected, eat a balanced diet, get good sleep, and keep her mind active with reading, puzzles, or hobbies. - **Routine check-ups:** At her next regular doctor visit, you could mention the forgetfulness. The doctor can check for reversible causes like vitamin deficiencies, thyroid problems, or medication side effects. **When to seek urgent help:** If Kamala suddenly becomes very confused, disoriented, can't recognize familiar people or places, or has trouble with her usual activities, see a doctor promptly. This is not a diagnosis, just guidance based on what you've shared. You're doing a great job keeping an eye on her wellbeing.

Q → kind info · about Kamala · 12215 ms
Some mild forgetfulness like occasionally misplacing keys or glasses can be a normal part of aging, especially over 80. This type of memory change is quite common. However, it's worth keeping an eye on whether it's getting worse or affecting her daily life more significantly. If you notice any of these changes, it would be worth seeing a doctor: • Getting lost in familiar places • Forgetting names of close family members or friends • Difficulty managing money, cooking, or other routine tasks she used to handle well • Repeating the same questions or stories within minutes • Confusion about time, dates, or where she is • Changes in mood, personality, or withdrawal from activities she used to enjoy • Difficulty following conversations or finding words Is Kamala's forgetfulness causing any problems with her day-to-day activities, or have you noticed it changing recently? I can ask a few questions to get a better sense of how she's doing.

**This needs urgent medical attention. Please take Kamala to the nearest emergency department now, or call for an ambulance.** Sudden confusion in an 80-year-old is a medical emergency. It can be a sign of serious conditions such as: - **Stroke** (blocked or bleeding blood vessel in the brain) - **Severe infection** (like a urinary tract infection or pneumonia causing delirium) - **Low blood sugar** or other metabolic problems - **Head injury** (even a minor fall can cause bleeding in the brain in elderly people) - **Heart or breathing problems** affecting oxygen to the brain **What to do right now:** - Get Kamala to emergency care immediately - Note the exact time the confusion started (this morning) - Check if she has had a fall, fever, or any other symptoms - Bring a list of any medicines she takes regularly **At the hospital**, doctors will examine her, check vital signs, and likely do blood tests and brain imaging to find the cause and start treatment quickly. Time is critical with conditions like stroke, so please don't delay. This is not a diagnosis, but sudden confusion in an elderly person always needs urgent medical evaluation.

User: I've been feeling a bit dizzy when I stand up since I started my BP tablets, should I just stop taking them?
Q → kind followup · about Suresh · episode e_4aa11aaf · 16367 ms
**Don't stop your BP tablets without talking to your doctor first.** Stopping blood pressure medication suddenly can be dangerous and cause your blood pressure to spike. What you're experiencing sounds like orthostatic hypotension (a drop in blood pressure when standing), which can happen when starting BP medication as your body adjusts. To help me guide you better, I need to know: 1. **When did you start the BP tablets?** (How many days/weeks ago?) 2. **How severe is the dizziness?** Does it make you feel like you might faint, or is it mild and passes quickly? 3. **Any other symptoms** with the dizziness, like blurred vision, feeling lightheaded, or actually fainting?

That's all very reassuring! Ved is showing good signs – no fever, happy, well-hydrated, and feeding well. **What it might be:** At 5 months old, a stuffy nose that started yesterday is most likely a common cold (viral upper respiratory infection). Babies can get congested easily because their nasal passages are so small, but Ved's body is handling it well. **What to do now:** • **Keep feeding normally** – breast or bottle feeds help keep him hydrated • **Saline nose drops** can help loosen mucus: put 1-2 drops in each nostril before feeds, then use a bulb syringe or let him sneeze it out • **Elevate the head** slightly during sleep (e.g. a small towel under the mattress – never pillows in the cot) • **Humidity** can help: a cool-mist humidifier in his room, or sit with him in a steamy bathroom for a few minutes • **No medicines** – cold and cough medicines are not safe for babies This should clear up on its own in 5-10 days. **When to seek urgent help:** Watch for any of these warning signs and go to a doctor or emergency department if Ved: • Has trouble breathing (fast breathing, chest pulling in, grunting, or flaring nostrils) • Stops feeding or is taking much less than usual • Has a fever (temperature 38°C or higher – fever in a baby under 6 months always needs medical review) • Becomes very sleepy, floppy, or difficult to wake • Has blue or pale lips or skin • Has a worsening cough or wheezing This is guidance only and not a diagnosis. If you're worried about Ved at any point, it's always okay to have him checked by a doctor.

The excellent signs are that he's breathing normally, feeding well, staying happy and hydrated—these tell me he's coping well with the stuffiness. **What to do now:** **Home care:** - **Saline nose drops:** Use baby saline drops (available at pharmacies) to help clear his nose. Put 1-2 drops in each nostril before feeds to make feeding easier. - **Upright position:** Hold him upright or slightly elevated during and after feeds—this can help with drainage. - **Humidity:** A cool mist humidifier in his room, or sitting with him in a steamy bathroom for a few minutes, can help loosen mucus. - **Keep feeding:** Continue regular feeds—breast milk or formula will keep him hydrated. - **Comfort:** Extra cuddles and comfort as needed! Stuffy noses in babies usually clear up on their own within 7-10 days. **When to seek urgent help** (go to the emergency department or call your doctor immediately) if Ved: - Has fast, difficult breathing or you hear wheezing - Refuses feeds or drinks much less than usual - Has fewer wet nappies (dehydration) - Develops a fever (38°C or higher—important for babies under 6 months) - Becomes very sleepy or hard to wake - Develops blue or pale lips or skin - The stuffiness lasts more than 10-14 days This is not a diagnosis, just guidance on what Ved's symptoms might mean and when to seek care.

That's all very reassuring! Ved is showing good signs – no fever, happy, well-hydrated, and feeding well. **What it might be:** At 5 months old, a stuffy nose that started yesterday is most likely a common cold (viral upper respiratory infection). Babies can get congested easily because their nasal passages are so small, but Ved's body is handling it well. **What to do now:** • **Keep feeding normally** – breast or bottle feeds help keep him hydrated • **Saline nose drops** can help loosen mucus: put 1-2 drops in each nostril before feeds, then use a bulb syringe or let him sneeze it out • **Elevate the head** slightly during sleep (e.g. a small towel under the mattress – never pillows in the cot) • **Humidity** can help: a cool-mist humidifier in his room, or sit with him in a steamy bathroom for a few minutes • **No medicines** – cold and cough medicines are not safe for babies This should clear up on its own in 5-10 days. **When to seek urgent help:** Watch for any of these warning signs and go to a doctor or emergency department if Ved: • Has trouble breathing (fast breathing, chest pulling in, grunting, or flaring nostrils) • Stops feeding or is taking much less than usual • Has a fever (temperature 38°C or higher – fever in a baby under 6 months always needs medical review) • Becomes very sleepy, floppy, or difficult to wake • Has blue or pale lips or skin • Has a worsening cough or wheezing This is guidance only and not a diagnosis. If you're worried about Ved at any point, it's always okay to have him checked by a doctor.

Good news — this sounds like a **mild common cold or possibly allergic rhinitis**. Since you have no fever, no breathing problems, you're eating and drinking normally, and you're otherwise healthy, this can be managed at home. **What to do:** • **Stay hydrated** – drink plenty of fluids (water, warm liquids like tea or soup) • **Rest** when you need it • **Saline nasal spray or rinse** can help clear congestion and make you more comfortable • **Over-the-counter antihistamines** (like cetirizine or loratadine) if it feels more like allergies, or a **decongestant** (as directed on the label) if you develop stuffiness — but don't use decongestant nasal sprays for more than 3 days • **Steam inhalation** may provide relief Most colds improve on their own within 7-10 days. **See a doctor if:** • You develop a high fever (above 38.5°C) • Severe headache or facial pain develops • You have trouble breathing or wheezing • Symptoms last more than 10 days or get worse instead of better • You develop thick green or yellow nasal discharge with facial pain This is not a diagnosis — just guidance on managing your symptoms. Feel better soon!

User: my neighbour's son just got stung by a bee and his face is swelling up and he's struggling to breathe
Q → kind assessment · urgency urgent · escalate True · about Neighbour's son · episode e_77333283 · 28664 ms
**This is a medical emergency – call your local emergency number (or 102/108 for ambulance in India) immediately or get him to the nearest emergency department now.** This sounds like a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to the bee sting. Facial swelling combined with breathing difficulty can rapidly become life-threatening as the airway can close off. **While waiting for emergency help:** - Keep him sitting upright (this helps breathing) - If he has an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen), use it immediately on the outer thigh - Loosen any tight clothing around the neck - Do NOT give anything to eat or drink - If he becomes unconscious but is breathing, place him on his side (recovery position) - If he stops breathing, start CPR if you know how **Do not delay – this requires immediate emergency medical care.** Time is critical with anaphylaxis. Even if symptoms improve slightly, he still needs emergency evaluation as reactions can worsen or return.

**This sounds like a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis). Call your local emergency number or get Aarav to the nearest emergency department immediately.** Swelling lips and wheezing after eating peanuts are signs of a serious allergic reaction that can get worse very quickly. **What to do RIGHT NOW:** • Call emergency services (ambulance) or go to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately • If Aarav has an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen), use it NOW and still go to the emergency department • Keep him sitting upright (helps with breathing) • Do not give him anything to eat or drink • Stay with him and watch for worsening symptoms **Go to emergency immediately if:** • Breathing becomes more difficult • Wheezing gets worse • He becomes very drowsy, confused, or unresponsive • Swelling spreads to his face or throat • His skin becomes pale or bluish • He collapses or faints Even if symptoms seem to improve, he needs emergency medical assessment because reactions can come back (biphasic reaction) hours later. This is a medical emergency - please act now and seek emergency care for Aarav.

Q → kind assessment · urgency urgent · escalate True · about neighbour's son · 16067 ms
**This is a medical emergency – call your local emergency number (108/102) or get him to the nearest emergency department immediately.** He is showing signs of a **severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)** to the bee sting. Facial swelling and difficulty breathing can progress rapidly and become life-threatening. **While waiting for help:** - Keep him as calm and still as possible - If he has an EpiPen or adrenaline auto-injector, use it now (inject into the outer thigh) - Help him sit upright if breathing is easier that way - Loosen tight clothing around the neck and chest - Do NOT give anything by mouth if he's struggling to breathe **Get emergency help NOW** – do not wait to see if it gets better. This needs immediate medical treatment.

Q → kind assessment · urgency urgent · escalate True · about Rajiv · episode e_643d7e8b · 20538 ms
**Rajiv, chest tightness that comes on with exertion and goes away with rest is a serious symptom that needs urgent medical attention.** Given your age (45), your family history (your father's heart attack at 50), and the classic pattern you describe — tightness triggered by physical activity like climbing stairs and relieved by rest — this could be **angina**, a sign that your heart muscle isn't getting enough blood when it's working harder. This warrants immediate evaluation. **What to do now:** **Go to the nearest emergency department or call your local emergency number today.** Do not wait. You need: - An ECG (heart tracing) - Blood tests to check for heart damage - Assessment by a doctor, likely a cardiologist While angina can be stable, it can also be a warning sign of a heart attack risk. Early evaluation and treatment can prevent serious complications. **Until you're seen:** - Avoid physical exertion - Do not drive yourself; have someone take you or call for emergency transport - If the tightness becomes severe, doesn't go away with rest, spreads to your arm/jaw/back, or you feel sweaty, short of breath, or nauseated, call emergency services immediately This is not a diagnosis, but chest discomfort with your pattern and risk factors requires urgent professional evaluation.

**This needs urgent medical attention.** The combination of breathlessness with minimal activity and tingling lips is concerning, especially as these symptoms have developed quickly. **Go to the nearest emergency department now or call your local emergency number** if you also have: - Difficulty speaking full sentences - Blue/grey tinge to your lips or face - Chest tightness or pain - Wheezing or noisy breathing - Facial or throat swelling - Worsening breathlessness Even without these, you should **see a doctor urgently today** — go to A&E or an urgent care clinic. **Possible causes:** - Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) - Acute asthma attack - Respiratory infection with complications - Anxiety/panic attack (though this needs to be ruled out by medical assessment) The tingling lips can indicate low oxygen levels or be part of an allergic reaction. While a runny nose might suggest a simple cold, breathlessness that limits normal activity after just one day is NOT typical and needs immediate medical evaluation. **Do not drive yourself** — have someone take you or call an ambulance if you're alone and symptoms worsen. This is not a diagnosis, and given the breathing difficulty, you need in-person medical assessment right away.
